source: Miller (1956) The magical number seven, plus or minus two: absolute judgment
finding: Absolute judgment of one-dimensional stimuli is limited by information, about 2.6 bits (about 6.5 categories). Memory span is limited by number of items, not bits.
numbers: Mean channel capacity 2.6 bits, SD 0.6, range about 3 to 15 categories. Pitch 2.5 bits (Pollack 1952), loudness 2.3 (Garner 1953), salt 1.9, position in interval 3.25. Digits carry 3.3 bits each; words about 10 bits. Span about 9 for binary digits, about 5 for monosyllabic words (Hayes).
quote: Absolute judgment is limited by the amount of information. Immediate memory is limited by the number of items.
limits: Review of other people's data, not new experiments. Miller called the shared 7 a possible 'pernicious, Pythagorean coincidence'. Span estimate is rough.
agent_relevance: The 7 is a loose range, not a constant. The budget unit for the agent should be the chunk, not the token or item.

source: Miller (1956) recoding and the chunk definition (Smith experiment)
finding: Span stays near 7 items while bits per item rise through recoding. A chunk is a familiar unit made by grouping input and giving the group a new name.
numbers: Smith (reported by Miller), 20 subjects: span 9 binary digits, 7 octal digits. Binary in triples recoded to octal. Smith recalled 12 octal digits = 36 binary; 2:1 recoding gave 24 binary, 4:1 and 5:1 about 40.
quote: organizing or grouping the input into familiar units or chunks
limits: One trained expert after long practice. The chunk is defined by use, not measured independently.
agent_relevance: Holding named summaries instead of raw text is the only route to more content under a fixed count. Matches summarise-and-label operators.

source: Miller (1956) subitizing and multidimensional judgments
finding: Adding dimensions raises total information but with sharply diminishing return per dimension.
numbers: Six acoustic dimensions together 7.2 bits (about 150 categories) vs 2.6 bits for one. Eight binary dimensions 6.9 bits. Kaufman 1949 dots flashed 1/5 s: no errors up to 5 or 6 dots.
limits: Cross-study comparison of different subjects and methods.
agent_relevance: Several small structured fields carry more than one long narrative field; analogy only.

source: Chase and Simon (1973) Perception in chess: recall by skill
finding: Chess skill gave better memory only for real game positions, not random ones. First-trial recall after a 5 s view: master about 16 pieces, class A about 8, beginner about 4 in middle games.
numbers: N = 3 players (master M, class A, beginner B). Middle games trial 1: about 16 / 8 / 4 pieces. End games about 8 / 7 / 4. Random positions: no relation to skill, and all three scored below the beginner's real-game result.
quote: In the random, unstructured positions there was no relation at all between memory of the position and playing strength.
limits: Only three subjects. Master recalled 16 of 25 pieces, below de Groot's 23 to 24 for grandmasters; authors blame less quiet positions.
agent_relevance: Expert advantage is stored structure in long-term memory, not a bigger buffer. Agent gains come from retrieved known patterns, not more context.

source: Chase and Simon (1973) chunk boundaries from pauses
finding: Pauses of about 2 s or more between placed pieces mark chunk boundaries. Pieces inside a chunk are linked by attack, defense, colour, proximity. A label sits in short-term memory and the content is fetched from long-term memory.
numbers: Within-glance intervals seldom over 2 s. About 2 s to recognise a chunk and store a label; about 300 ms per added element (Dansereau 1969). Pieces per chunk, perception task: 2.0 / 2.8 / 2.0 (M, A, B); memory task 2.5 / 2.1 / 1.9.
limits: Boundary rule depends on the pause criterion. Master recognised 4 of 9 new positions within 1 s, yet recall was the same (83% vs 79%).
agent_relevance: Supports the pointer view: working memory holds labels, the long-term store holds content. Mirrors fetching a stored note by key.

source: Chase and Simon (1973) chunk count versus skill
finding: Number of chunks stayed within the 7 plus or minus 2 span, but was NOT constant across skill: the master recalled more chunks and larger chunks.
numbers: Chunks per first trial, middle games: M 7.7, A 5.7, B 5.3. End games: M 7.6, A 6.4, B 4.2. First chunk size M 3.8 vs B 2.4 pieces; later chunks shrink toward 1 to 2.
quote: short-term memory consists of a linear list of seven or so unrelated chunk slots
limits: Authors raise that M may reconstruct from general knowledge; chunk count depends on a criterion separating recall from reconstruction (pauses over 10 s, or 5 s with errors).
agent_relevance: A flat fixed-slot story fails even in the founding chess data. Chunks can be organised into higher structure, so plan hierarchical notes.

source: Cowan (2010) The magical mystery four: capacity numbers
finding: Capacity is about 3 to 5 chunks in young adults when rehearsal and grouping are blocked. Miller's 7 reflects chunking and rehearsal.
numbers: Running span: last 3 to 5 digits. Rehearsal covers about 2 s of speech. Chen and Cowan: about 3 units with rehearsal blocked, singletons or learned pairs. Saults and Cowan: about 4 after masking sensory memory. Age 7: about 1.5 items vs about 3.0 for older children and adults. Longer verbal chunks (idioms) give 3 or 4 (Gilchrist 2008).
quote: a central memory store limited to 3 to 5 meaningful items in young adults
limits: Competing view: low-span people store more irrelevant material, so part of the limit is attention filtering (Kane 2001, Vogel 2005). Chen and Cowan dated 'in press' in the source.
agent_relevance: A hard cap near four live units means per-step state should be small and named.

source: Cowan (2010) why the limit exists
finding: Two camps: limit as weakness (neural firing cycles cannot keep more than about four concepts active) vs limit as strength (search is most efficient at about 3.5 items per group; small stores help learn rules).
numbers: No new data. Mathematical models of problem solving fit a working-memory size near 4.
limits: Argument level. Cowan and Rouder defend a fixed limit against the view that attention spreads thinly over items.
agent_relevance: A small working set may help search; more simultaneous items is not automatically better.

source: Luck and Vogel (2013) Visual working memory capacity review
finding: Visual change detection shows 3 to 4 objects, and multi-feature objects are held about as well as single-feature ones (object-based storage). Capacity tracks general intelligence.
numbers: Kmax about 3 to 4 colored squares. VWM capacity explains about 43% of fluid intelligence variance (Fukuda 2010) and about 46% of a broad battery (Johnson 2013). Test-retest r = 0.77 over 1.5 years. Schizophrenia (99) vs controls (77): d = 1.11. CDA amplitude rises with set size and plateaus at 3 to 4.
quote: a capacity of only 3-4 objects' worth of information
limits: Review by authors of the paradigm; intelligence figures are correlations in specific samples.
agent_relevance: In people, small-capacity differences predict reasoning. The same link for LLM scaffolds is untested here.

source: Zhang and Luck (2008) mixture model and the slots vs resources dispute, as summarised by Luck and Vogel (2013)
finding: Slots-plus-averaging mixture model: raising set size from 3 to 6 mainly lowers the chance an item is in memory (Pmem); precision (SD) barely changes. Bays and Husain 2008 resource reading was explained by guessing (Thiele 2011).
numbers: Zhang and Luck 2011: observers could not raise Kmax by trading precision, even with monetary incentives. Precision rises with set size up to Kmax, then levels off (Anderson 2011).
limits: Secondary reading. Slots vs resources is still contested (Donkin et al. 2016 title: resources masquerading as slots).
agent_relevance: If capacity is count-limited, spreading effort over many items does not help; selecting fewer items does.

source: Norris, Kalm and Hall (2020) Chunking and redintegration in verbal short-term memory
finding: Six experiments: small chunks (2 words) behave like redintegration (long-term memory helps rebuild a decayed trace); larger chunks (3 words) behave like data compression (Miller's recoding). Recoding has a cost.
numbers: Six experiments, 2AFC recognition and immediate serial recall; lists fixed at 7 words with varying chunk count. In Experiment 5, if one word of a learned triple was recalled, the chance all three were recalled was .94.
limits: Verbal lists with learned or acronym chunks. Direct support for compression came from only two earlier studies (Brady 2009, Thalmann 2019).
agent_relevance: Chunks of size 2 save no working space; the benefit may need triples or larger meaningful units.

source: Chen and Cowan (2005, 2009) and Cowan et al. (2012) as reported by Norris et al. (2020): chunk-based limit fails under strict scoring
finding: Four learned pairs gave twice the items of four singletons only under lenient scoring. Under strict serial-position scoring item count also depended on list length. Without articulatory suppression there was no chunk-based limit.
numbers: Chen and Cowan 2009 lists: 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 singletons or 4 or 6 pairs. Chen and Cowan 2005: eight singles = four pairs for eight-item lists. Conclusion cited from p. 1425.
quote: There is no apparent chunk-based constant capacity for strict serial recall
limits: Read through a later paper, not the originals. Cowan et al. 2012 extended to more list lengths and chunk sizes.
agent_relevance: A constant chunk budget holds for content recall, not for order. Do not assume order survives when more items are packed.

source: Mathy, Chekaf and Cowan (2018) Simple and complex working memory tasks allow similar benefits of compression
finding: The prediction that complex span (4 plus or minus 1) is lower than simple span (7 plus or minus 2) because interleaved processing blocks chunking was NOT confirmed. Compression helped both task types to a similar extent.
numbers: N = 94 students. Chunkability of coloured 3D shapes set by compressibility. Predicted task by chunkability interaction not found.
limits: Visual artificial stimuli. Authors say complex span may overestimate storage and the 7 vs 4 gap lies in some other mechanism.
agent_relevance: The 7 vs 4 gap cannot be put down to chunking alone; keep both numbers as ranges.

source: Jones (2012) Why chunking should be considered as an explanation for developmental change
finding: A chunking model of non-word repetition reproduces apparent growth in short-term memory capacity and processing speed without changing those parameters.
numbers: Model learns phoneme-sequence chunks; each chunk costs about 400 ms to encode; adjacent reliably encoded chunks merge. Performance improves with exposure and matches child data.
limits: Simulation, not new human data. A caution that capacity differences may be chunk knowledge differences.
agent_relevance: Gains can come from stored chunks rather than a bigger window; favours adding stored patterns over enlarging context.

source: Wikipedia, Chunking (psychology): summary of Ericsson, Chase and Faloon (1980) and others
finding: Student SF raised digit span from 7 to almost 80 over about 20 months (at least 230 hours). Authors credited mnemonic associations in long-term memory, not bigger short-term capacity; SF still chunked only 3 to 4 digits at a time.
numbers: Also lists Dirlam 1972 (chunks of 3 or 4 most efficient), Kibbe and Feigenson 2015 (14-month-olds hold 4 objects as 2 tokens of 2 categories, not 4 of one), Chekaf, Cowan and Mathy 2016 (compressibility and order).
limits: Secondary source; the original Science paper was not opened. Says 'almost 80', not 79.
agent_relevance: Huge span gains come from long-term retrieval structures, not from a larger window.

source: Chai, Abd Hamid and Abdullah (2018) Working memory from the psychological and neurosciences perspectives (review of Baddeley and Hitch model)
finding: Multi-component model: phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive; episodic buffer added in 2000. Cowan's embedded-process view: working memory is the attended part of activated long-term memory.
numbers: No capacity numbers in the portion read (first 100000 characters).
limits: Review only. Original 1974 dual-task data not read.
agent_relevance: Separate holders for verbal state and structured state, and a controller that should be code, fit the component split.

source: Gong, Wan and Wang (2024) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT (AAAI)
finding: gpt-3.5-turbo on verbal n-back shows a human-like drop with n. Detection sensitivity d' falls to about 1 at n = 3 in three of four verbal variants; added noise lowers capacity.
numbers: 50 blocks per n in {1,2,3}, temperature 1. Variants: base, noise (3 to 6 noise characters), feedback, reasoning. Larger spatial grids gave higher capacity.
limits: One API model for the main result; short sequences; mechanism claim is speculative.
agent_relevance: N-back probes can measure how many updated items the agent tracks. Strip distractors before working steps.

source: Gong et al. (2024) model comparison on verbal n-back
finding: GPT-4 far exceeds GPT-3.5. Six open models (Bloomz-7B, ChatGLM-6B v1.0 and v1.1, Vicuna-7B and 13B) had very low capacity and were nearly indistinguishable.
numbers: Eight models in total; base verbal n-back only; GPT-4 tested only to n = 3 for cost, so its limit is not located.
limits: Single task. The human-likeness claim rests on curve shape, not a fitted model.
agent_relevance: Working-memory-like limits scale with model strength; set chunk size per model.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the middle (TACL)
finding: Accuracy is highest when the relevant document is first or last and lowest in the middle. Extended-context models did no better when the input fit in both windows.
numbers: 10, 20 and 30 documents. Closed-book / oracle accuracy: GPT-3.5-Turbo 56.1% / 88.3%; Claude-1.3 48.3% / 76.1%; LongChat-13B 35.0% / 83.4%; MPT-30B 31.5% / 81.9%. GPT-3.5 accuracy drops over 20% by position and with 20 to 30 documents can fall below its 56.1% no-document score.
quote: performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end
limits: 2023 models. Newer models may behave differently. The serial-position look is not shown to share a mechanism with human primacy and recency.
agent_relevance: Put the active material at the start or end of the prompt. Context length is not working capacity.

source: Levy, Jacoby and Goldberg (2024) Same task, more tokens
finding: Reasoning accuracy falls as padding grows even when the needed facts are unchanged. Average accuracy drops from 0.92 to 0.68 by 3000 tokens.
numbers: Input 250 to 3000 tokens, key paragraphs fixed, similar or dissimilar padding. Long-input next-word-prediction performance is uncorrelated with long-input reasoning accuracy. Chain of thought lifts accuracy by a similar amount at every length (exception GPT-4, where the gap grows).
limits: Synthetic QA. Failure modes: no answer, answer before reasoning, bias toward false.
agent_relevance: Length costs accuracy far below the context limit: keep each step's input small. Chain of thought does not repair this.

source: Hsieh et al. (2024) RULER: what is the real context size of your long-context language models (COLM)
finding: Claimed context length overstates usable length. Almost all of 17 models fall below a Llama2-7B-at-4K baseline of 85.6% before their claimed length.
numbers: 13 tasks, 4K to 128K. GPT-4: 96.6, 96.3, 95.2, 93.2, 87.0, 81.2 at 4K to 128K; claimed 128K, effective 64K. Llama3.1-70B: 96.5 at 4K to 66.6 at 128K, effective 64K. Gemini-1.5-Pro: 96.7 to 94.4, effective above 128K. LongChat-7B: effective under 4K at claimed 32K.
limits: Threshold for effective length is arbitrary; mostly open models; newer models have moved.
agent_relevance: Plan per-step context against measured effective length, not the headline window.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation
finding: When a task is delivered in pieces over turns, 15 LLMs lose about 39% on average compared with one-shot. The loss is mostly unreliability, not aptitude.
numbers: 15 LLMs, 6 tasks, 600 instructions, 10 simulations each. Figure 1: aptitude -15%, unreliability +112%. Table 1 average degradation -39%. Named causes: verbose replies, premature answers, wrong assumptions, over-reliance on earlier turns.
limits: Simulated users; averages hide model differences; link to human chunk limits is analogy.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model carry state across turns. The program holds state and restates the full problem each step.

source: Baddeley and Hitch (1974) original dual-task data (not opened)
finding: Not read this session. Background recall only: a digit preload slowed reasoning when large, which led to separate subsystems plus a central executive. Do not cite numbers.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Original not reachable; to be checked by another angle.
agent_relevance: None until verified.

source: Gobet et al. (2001) Chunking mechanisms in human learning (not opened)
finding: Not read this session. Background recall only: reviews chunk models such as EPAM, CHREST, Soar, ACT-R.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Full text not reachable.
agent_relevance: None until verified.

source: Gobet and Simon (1998) template theory (not opened)
finding: Not read this session. Background recall only: experts hold large templates with fillable slots, to explain recall beyond a few chunks.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Full text not reachable.
agent_relevance: A structured note with variable slots is the analogue; untested.
